Analysis of the two-for-one swap heuristic for approximating the maximum independent set in a _k_-polymatroid<sup>∗</sup>

**Abstract**

Let \(f:2^N\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) be a polymatroid (an integer-valued non-decreasing submodular set function with \(f(\emptyset)=0\)). A _k_-polymatroid satisfies that \(f(e)\le k\) for all \(e\in N\). We call \(S\subseteq N\) _independent_ if \(f(S)=\sum_{e\in S}f(e)\) and _f(e)\>_0 for all \(e\in S\). Such a set was also called a _matching_. Finding a maximum-size independent set in a 2-polymatroid has been studied and polynomial-time algorithms are known for linearly represented polymatroids. For \(k\ge 3\), the problem is NP-hard, and a \(((2/k)-\epsilon)\)-approximation is known and is obtained by swapping as long as possible a subset of up to \((1/\epsilon)^{log_{k-1}(2k+1)}\) elements from the current solution by a set with one more element.

Here we give a simple analysis of the more particular two-for-one repeated swapping heuristic, obtaining a tight (weaker) (2/(_k_+1))-approximation.

**Keywords:** Approximation Algorithm; Matroid; Local Optimization. **2000 MSC:** 05B35; 05B40; 68W05; 68W25; 68W40; 68R05; 90C27.

## 1 Introduction

A polymatroid \(f:2^N\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) on a ground set _N_ is a non-decreasing (monotone) integer-valued submodular function with \(f(\emptyset)=0\). A function _f_ is monotone iff \(f(A)\le f(B)\) for all \(A\subseteq B\). A function _f_ is submodular iff \(f(A)+f(B)\ge f(A\cup B)+f(A\cap B)\) for all _A_, \(B\subseteq N\).<sup>1</sup> Polymatroids generalize matroids which have the additional condition that \(f(\{i\})\le 1\) for all \(i\in N\).

Matroids are versatile mathematical structures that generalize numerous combinatorial models, including matching \[28, 29\], online computation \[3, 2\], diversity maximization \[1\] and variants of clustering problems \[8, 25, 26, 40\].

A _k_-polymatroid satisfies that \(f(e)\le k\) for all \(e\in N\). We call \(S\subseteq N\) _independent_ if \(f(S)=\sum_{e\in S}f(e)\) and _f(e)\>_0 for all \(e\in S\). Such a set was also called a _matching_ by \[33\]. The MAXIMUM INDEPENDENT SET IN A _k_-POLYMATROID (or MISkP) asks for finding a maximum-size independent set in a _k_-polymatroid. Finding maximum-size sets in downward- closed set systems is one of the most fundamental combinatorial optimization problems \[10, 38\].

MISkP was also studied under the name of Matroid _k_-Parity. MIS2P has been proposed by Lawler \[28\] and polynomial-time algorithms are known for linearly represented polymatroids \[36, 32, 9, 15\]. There are 2-polymatroids for which MIS2P is NP-hard \[38\], and Jensen and Korte \[24\] have shown that there exists no algorithm in which the matroid is represented by an independence test oracle (or an oracle polynomially related to an independence test oracle) and which solves the problem in question after a number of calls on the oracle which is bounded by a polynomial in the number of elements of the ground set of the matroid.

Lee, Sviridenko, and Vondrák \[29\] give a polynomial-time approximation scheme for MIS2P using the local search method: start with a feasible current solution, and as long as we obtain a feasible solution, swap a subset of up to _j_ elements of the current solution by a set containing one more element. The algorithm stops when no such swap is possible. Precisely, to get a \((1-\epsilon)\)- approximation, they use a _j_ that is exponential in \(1/\epsilon\). For MISkP with \(k\ge 3\), \[29\] obtain a \(((2/k)-\epsilon)\)-approximation for this swapping heuristic with \(j=\lceil(1/\epsilon)^{log_{k-1}(2k+1)}\rceil\) (\[29\] only discusses the case where _f(e_)=_k_ for all \(e\in N\), the _k_-uniform case, but after deleting elements with _f(e_)=0, one can set \(f'(X)=f(X)+\sum_{e\in X}(k-f(e))\), so that \(f'(e)=k\) for all remaining _e_ and a set is independent with respect to _f_ if and only if it is independent with respect to \(f'\)). Note that \(log_{k-1}(2k+1)\le 3\) and for large _k_, it is close to 1. It is also known that a ratio better than \(\Omega(logk/k)\) is not possible unless _P=NP_ \[18\].

In this paper, we study this local-swap heuristic with _j_=1 and obtain a tight approximation ratio of 2/(_k_+1). This is weaker than the bound of \[29\], and MISkP is most useful when _k_ is small (i.e. MIS3P may help with Maximum Planar Subgraph \[6\] and related problems where MIS2P is used for the best known approximation). We have a simple proof for our (weaker) result which may open the way for proving a \(((2/k)-\epsilon)\)-approximation with swapping fewer elements, because for fixed \(k\ge 3\), \(j=O(log(1/\epsilon))\) suffices for the much simpler case of finding a maximum matching in a _k_-hypergraph \[21\]. Also, one can further try to apply the method of Cygan \[11\] with the goal of a \(((3/(k+1))-\epsilon)\)-approximation. Our method is based on exchange properties of Greene and Magnanti \[17\] (with special cases in \[16, 5\], also Exercise 8.48 in \[10\]) and a particular (base) case of the analysis of Hurkens and Schrijver \[21\].

As explained in \[29\], MISkP can approximately solve a number of other problems such as finding the maximum-size set that is independent in _k_ given matroids on the same ground set, which we call the _k_-Matroid Intersection Problem. 2-Matroid Intersection is a classical combinatorial optimization problem that admits polynomial-time algorithms \[13, 38\]. Previous to \[29\], _k_-Matroid<tbc>

<tbc>Intersection had a approximation ratio of 1/(_k_-1) \[27\].

We do mention that only unweighted problems were discussed before. Edmonds \[12\] (also in \[38\]) gives exact polynomial-time algorithms for Max-Weight 2-Matroid Intersection. For weighted MIS2P in linearly represented matroids \[7, 37\] give pseudopolynomial algorithms and approximation schemes, and Iwata and Kobayashi \[23\] gives a polynomial-time algorithm. Linhares, Olver, Swamy, and Zenklusen \[30\] gives a (1/2)-approximation for Max-Weight 3-Matroid Intersection.

## 2 Preliminaries

In the introduction, a matroid was defined as a polymatroid which has the additional condition that \(f(\{i\})\le 1\) for all \(i\in N\). An alternative definition is: A _matroid_ (defined in \[10, 38\]) is an ordered pair _M_=(_E,_I) satisfying the following conditions:

1. _E_ is a nonempty finite set.<tbc>

2. I is a nonempty family of subsets of _E_, called _independent_ subsets of _E_, such that if \(B\in\mathcal{I}\) and \(A\subseteq B\), then \(A\in\mathcal{I}\).<tbc>

3. If \(A\in\mathcal{I},B\in\mathcal{I}\), and |_A|\<|B_|, then there exists some element \(x\in B\backslash A\) such that \(A\cup\{x\}\in\mathcal{I}\).

To construct _M_=(_E,_I) from the polymatroid _f_, let _E=N_ and I be the sets that are defined as independent in the polymatroid _f_. It is known \[38\] and not hard to prove that the three conditions above hold, assuming that \(f(\{i\})\le 1\) for all \(i\in N\). To construct a polymatroid from the alternative definition above, for set \(A\subseteq E\), define the _rank_ function \(r(A)=\mathrm{max}_{B\subseteq A}\) and \(_{B\in\mathcal{I}}|B|\). This definition implies that \(A\in\mathcal{I}\) if and only if |_A_|=_r(A_). It is not hard to prove (see \[38\]) that _r_() is a monotone submodular function with \(r(\emptyset)=0\), and thus _r_ is a polymatroid. Also, \(r(\{i\})\le 1\) for all \(i\in E\).

Given a matroid _M_=(_E,_I), we say that \(A\in\mathcal{I}\) is a maximal independent subset of _M_, or a _basis_ of _M_ if there exists no \(x\in E\backslash A\) such that \(A\cup\{x\}\in\mathcal{I}\). It is known that all bases of a matroid have the same size. We will use:

**Theorem 2.1** (Theorem 3.3 of \[17\])**.** _Consider a matroid and let Q,P be two of its bases. Let X_<sub>1</sub>_,X_<sub>2</sub>_,...,X<sub>t</sub> be a partition of Q. Then there is a partition Y_<sub>1</sub>_,Y_<sub>2</sub>_,...,Y<sub>t</sub> of P such that for all i_=1,2_,...,t,_ \((Q\backslash X_i)\cup Y_i\) _is a basis._

Given matroid _M_=(_E,_I) and \(Z\subseteq E\), let _X_ be a maximal independent subset of _Z_. Let \(M/Z=(E',\mathcal{I}')\) where \(E'=E\backslash Z\) and \(\mathcal{I}'=\{A\subseteq E'\big|A\cup X\in\mathcal{I}\}\). We call _M/Z_ the _contraction_ of _M_ by set _Z_ (it is known and not hard to prove that the choice of _X_ does not matter). The rank function \(r'\) of _M/Z_ satisfies \(r'(Y)=r(Y\cup Z)-r(Z)\) (this is not hard to see, and appears in \[38\]).<tbc>

Helgason \[19\], McDiarmid \[34\], and Lovasz \[31\] have shown that for any polymatroid on set _N_ given by function _f_ there exists a matroid _M_=(_E,_I) with rank function _r_ with the following properties: Every element \(h\in N\) is associated with an independent set \(M_h\subseteq E\), all the _M<sub>h</sub>_ are pairwise disjoint, and for all \(X\subseteq N\) we have \(f(X)=r(\cup_{h\in X}M_h)\). This exact set of conditions occurs in \[38\] at subsection 44.6b. Although we use this underlying structure of polymatroids for our analysis, at no point is it necessary to run the algorithm.

## 3 The analysis of the two-for-one swap heuristic

We first set up the matroid in which we will apply Theorem 2.1; this is taken from \[29\] with slightly changed (clarified) notation (for this set up, we had another method based on Theorem 2.1 before we discovered \[29\]).

Let \(A\subseteq N\) be our current solution and \(B\subseteq N\) be an optimum solution. Assume no feasible addition or two-for-one swap is possible, from this we will prove that \(|A|\ge(2/(k+1))|B|\). If \(A=\emptyset\), the absence of a feasible addition implies \(B=\emptyset\); assume henceforth that \(A\neq\emptyset\). Let _M_ be the matroid with the rank function _r_ associated to the polymatroid on _N_ defined by _f_() as explained at the end of the previous section. Let \(\overline{A}=\cup_{h\in A}M_h\) and \(\overline{B}=\cup_{h\in B}M_h\). We remove from _M_ all elements outside of \(\overline{A}\cup\overline{B}\) as we will not use them for our analysis. We have \(r(\overline{A})=f(A)=\sum_{h\in A}f(h)=\sum_{h\in A}r(M_h)=\sum_{h\in A}|M_h|=|\overline{A}|\), where the first equality is from the definition of _M_, the second equality is from the fact that _A_ is independent in the polymatroid, the third equality is again from the properties of _M_, the fourth equality is from the fact that each _M<sub>h</sub>_ is independent in _M_ (as seen in the properties of _M_), and the last equality from the fact that the sets _M<sub>h</sub>_ are pairwise disjoint (as seen in the properties of _M_). We conclude that <o>_A_</o> is independent in _M_. The same reasoning is applied to obtain that <o>_B_</o> is independent in _M_.

Since <o>_A_</o> is independent in _M_, we have a maximal independent set \(\bar{I}\) in _M_ that contains <o>_A_</o>. Define \(\overline{B^{^\prime}}=\bar{I}\backslash\overline{A}\); as the ground set of _M_ is \(\overline{A}\cup\overline{B}\), we have that \(\overline{B^{^\prime}}\subseteq\overline{B}\). From here our analysis diverges from \[29\]. Contract \(\overline{B^{^\prime}}\) in _M_ to obtain matroid \(M'\). Let \(\overline{B^{^{\prime\prime}}}:=\overline{B}\backslash\overline{B^{^\prime}}\). As \(\overline{B^{^\prime}}\) is independent in _M_, by the definition of contraction, the independence of set <o>_A_</o> in \(M'\) corresponds to the independence of \(\overline{A}\cup\overline{B^{^\prime}}\) in _M_. Also, the independence of \(\overline{B^{^{\prime\prime}}}\) in \(M'\) corresponds to the independence of \(\overline{B^{^{\prime\prime}}}\cup\overline{B^{^\prime}}=\overline{B}\) in _M_. As \(\overline{A}\cup\overline{B^{^\prime}}\) is a basis in _M_, <o>_A_</o> is a basis in \(M'\), and similarly <o>_B_</o> being independent in _M_ implies that \(\overline{B^{^{\prime\prime}}}\) is an independent set in \(M'\). As such \(\overline{B^{^{\prime\prime}}}\subseteq\overline{C}\) for some basis <o>_C_</o> in \(M'\). See Figure 1 for an illustration.

Let _a_=|_A_|. With _A_={_h_<sub>1</sub>_,h_<sub>2</sub>_,...,h<sub>a</sub>_}, we have that _M_<sub>_h_<sub>1</sub></sub>_,M_<sub>_h_<sub>2</sub></sub>_,...,M<sub>h<sub>a</sub></sub>_ is a partition of <o>_A_</o>. Use Theorem 2.1 to obtain a partition _Y_<sub>1</sub>_,Y_<sub>2</sub>_,...,Y<sub>a</sub>_ of <o>_C_</o> such that, for all \(i\in\{1,2,\dots,a\}\), we have that \(\overline{A}\backslash M_{h_i}\cup Y_i\) is a basis in \(M'\). As all bases have the same size, \(|Y_i|\ge|M_{h_i}|\) for every _i_. Since \(\sum_i|Y_i|=|\overline{C}|=|\overline{A}|=\sum_i|M_{h_i}|\), equality holds for every _i_; consequently, \(Y_i\cap(\overline{A}\backslash M_{h_i})=\emptyset\). Construct a bipartite graph _G_ with parts _A_ and _B_, with an exception: for each element in both _A_ and _B_, duplicate it and put it in both parts of _G_. In _G_, we put an edge between \(h_i\in A\) and \(e_j\in B\) if \(M_{e_j}\cap Y_i\neq\emptyset\). See Figure 2 for an illustration. Call a vertex of degree 1 in _G_ a singleton.

If \(h_i\in A\cap B\), then \(M_{h_i}\subseteq\overline{B^{^{\prime\prime}}}\subseteq\overline{C}\). The preceding disjointness and equal sizes imply _Y<sub>i</sub>=M<sub>h<sub>i</sub></sub>_. Thus the two copies of _h<sub>i</sub>_ form an isolated edge in _G_.

If a vertex of \(e\in B\) has degree 0 in _G_, then \(M_e\cap Y_i=\emptyset\) for all \(h_i\in A\), which implies that \(M_e\subseteq\overline{B^{^{\prime\prime}}}\), and this implies that \(A\cup\{e\}\) is independent in the polymatroid on _N_ given by _f_(). This cannot happen when the two-for-one heuristic stops. We conclude that every vertex of _B_ has degree at least one in _G_.

We claim that we cannot have a vertex of _A_ adjacent in _G_ to two singletons in _B_. Indeed, assume that \(h_i\in A\) is adjacent to _e_ and _f_ distinct singleton vertices of _B_. Then \(A':=A\backslash\{h_i\}\cup\{e,f\}\) has size |_A_|+1, since the isolated-edge property gives \(e,f\notin A\), and is an independent set, as we argue next. _e_ being a singleton implies that all elements of \(M_e\cap\overline{B^{^{\prime\prime}}}\) are in _Y<sub>i</sub>_. Same reasoning applies to _f_. Therefore \(\cup_{g\in A^\prime} M_g\subseteq\left(\overline{A}\backslash M_{h_i}\cup Y_i\right)\cup\left(M_e\cap\overline{B^{^{\prime\prime}}}\right)\cup\left(M_f\cap\overline{B^{^{\prime\prime}}}\right)\subseteq\left(\overline{A}\backslash M_{h_i}\cup Y_i\right)\cup\overline{B^{^{\prime\prime}}}\). As \(\overline{A}\backslash M_{h_i}\cup Y_i\) is a basis in \(M'\), we have that \(\left(\overline{A}\backslash M_{h_i}\cup Y_i\right)\cup\overline{B^{^{\prime\prime}}}\) is independent in _M_, and from this we deduce that \(\cup_{g\in A^\prime} M_g\) is independent in _M_, which implies that \(A'\) is independent in the polymatroid on _N_ given by _f_(). This cannot happen when the two-for-one heuristic stops.

Now we compare |_A_| with |_B_| using the arguments from the base case (Case 2) in the proof of Theorem 1 of \[21\]. In _G_, the degree of a vertex \(h_i\in A\) is at most _k_, as \(|Y_i|=|M_{h_i}|=f(h_i)\le k\) and _M<sub>e<sub>j</sub></sub>_ is disjoint from _M<sub>e<sub>l</sub></sub>_, for \(e_j\neq e_l\), \(e_j,e_l\in B\). Partition _B_ into _S_ and _D_, where _S_ is the set of singletons in _B_, and _D_ are the remaining vertices of _G_ that are in _B_. All the vertices in _D_ have degree at least two, and thus \(k|A|\ge|E(G)|\ge|S|+2|D|\). From the previous paragraph, \(|A|\ge|S|\). Add these two last equations and obtain that \((k+1)|A|\ge 2|B|\), which implies the ratio of at least 2/(_k_+1) for the two-for-one swap heuristic.

**Note.** It may be more intuitive to contract \(\overline{A}\cap\overline{B}\) early in the proof, but readjusting the definitions will make this proof longer.

**Tightness.** \[21\] prove tight bounds and from their proof we can immediately obtain that the approximation algorithm of the two-for-one swap heuristic is exactly 2/(_k_+1). For _k_=1, every maximal independent set is optimum; assume \(k\ge 2\) below. Assume that _N_ consists of collection of subsets of _k_ points from some universe _U_, and \(f(A)=|\cup_{e\in A}e|\). It is well known (and easy to show) that _f_() is increasing submodular and so we do have a MISkP instance. In this setting, a set \(A\subseteq N\) is independent if and only if the elements of _A_ are disjoint. (this is the _k_-Set Packing problem \[21, 11, 18\]). Let _e_<sub>1</sub>_,e_<sub>2</sub>_,...,e_<sub>_k_+1</sub> be _k_+1 disjoint sets of _U_ with _k_ elements each, and let _e_<sub>_k_+2</sub> have one element from each of _e_<sub>1</sub>_,e_<sub>3</sub>_,e_<sub>4</sub>_,...,e_<sub>_k_+1</sub> and _e_<sub>_k_+3</sub> be disjoint from _e_<sub>_k_+2</sub> and have one element from each of _e_<sub>2</sub>_,e_<sub>3</sub>_,e_<sub>4</sub>_,...,e_<sub>_k_+1</sub>. The heuristic can stop with {_e_<sub>_k_+2</sub>_,e_<sub>_k_+3</sub>} as the output while a solution with _k_+1 elements of _N_ exists: {_e_<sub>1</sub>_,...,e_<sub>_k_+1</sub>}. This example for _k_=3 is given in Figure 3.

### Method Limitations

We are not able to construct this bipartite graph for larger swaps and general matroids (or linear matroids). The method does work for strongly base orderable matroids \[4, 22, 14, 39, 20\] and gives the better dependence of \[21\] of the approximation ratio as function of the size of the swap. Constructing such a bipartite graph for strongly base orderable matroids was done in Feldman, Naor, Schwartz, and Ward \[14\], but we could not find an explicit dependence of the approximation ratio as a function of the size of the swap in their paper. Note that the matroid being strongly base orderable or not does not affect the algorithm, just its proven performance guarantee.
